item.title: A stem-like CD8+ T cell reservoir resists exhaustion and sustains alloimmunity a decade after transplantation
item.dc:creator: Dawei Zou
Yulin Dai
Stephanie G. Yi
Shuang Li
Luan Truong
Lillian W. Gaber
Richard J. Knight
Xiang Xiao
item.description:
Authors: Dawei Zou, Yulin Dai, Stephanie G. Yi, Shuang Li, Luan Truong, Lillian W. Gaber, Richard J. Knight, Xiang Xiao, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Chronic antigen exposure is commonly thought to drive CD8 + T cells toward exhaustion. However, in transplantation, we show that sustained immunity is maintained by a persistent stem-like reservoir that iteratively replenishes short-lived cytotoxic effectors rather than progressing toward exhaustion. Analysis of rejected human kidney allografts obtained approximately 10 years after transplantation reveals extensive overlap of CD8 + T-cell clonotypes between the circulation and allografts. These clones are maintained in a TCF1 + stem-like state in the circulation but differentiate into TCF1 − cytotoxic effectors within allografts. Mouse models demonstrate that cytotoxic effector differentiation is restrained by TCF1 and depends on lactate dehydrogenase A. Cytotoxic effectors are short-lived and insufficient to mediate allograft rejection upon transfer into secondary hosts, whereas stem-like T cells retain self-renewal capacity, continuously replenish cytotoxic effectors, and drive rejection across serial transplantations. These findings establish a principle whereby a stem-like CD8 + T-cell reservoir drives sustained alloimmunity through continuous effector differentiation.

item.title: Layer-by-layer water filling in molecular-scale capillaries monitored by AFM
item.dc:creator: Mingwei Chen
Jingshan Wang
Artem Mishchenko
Ivan Timokhin
Qi Ge
Fengchao Wang
Andre K. Geim
Qian Yang
item.description:
Authors: Mingwei Chen, Jingshan Wang, Artem Mishchenko, Ivan Timokhin, Qi Ge, Fengchao Wang, Andre K. Geim, Qian Yang
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Under ambient humidity, water spontaneously condenses in pores only a few nanometers in size, making nanoscale capillarity central to numerous natural phenomena and technological applications. At these dimensions, water may no longer be treated as a continuous fluid, yet the consequences of molecular discreteness for capillary condensation and filling remain poorly understood. Here we study two-dimensional (2D) nanocapillaries fabricated by van der Waals assembly and, using atomic force microscopy (AFM), monitor their wall deformations during humidity-driven water uptake. We observe two distinct regimes: layer-by-layer filling of flexible capillaries and abrupt filling of more rigid ones. Flexible walls deform in ≈3 Å steps, consistent with the entry of individual molecular layers of water. The different filling regimes are explained by a competition between wall deformation energy and oscillatory wall-water interactions. These results, together with the theoretical framework developed here, show how molecular discreteness can profoundly affect ubiquitous capillary phenomena, with wall rigidity determining whether this discreteness is exposed or hidden within an apparently classical, Kelvin-like response.

item.title: High-performance devices from lab-scale to micro module directed by vertical PbI2 homogeneous growth perovskite films
item.dc:creator: Minhuan Wang
Yepin Zhao

item.description:
Authors: Minhuan Wang, Yepin Zhao, Zhenyang Suo, Chenyue Wang, Pengfei Wang, Bingying Xu, Zhenhuang Su, Jiming Bian, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The morphology of the initial PbI 2 film is very pivotal in dictating the uniformity and crystallinity of the resultant perovskite film in the two-step sequential deposition processes. A solution-based induction is introduced to transform PbI 2 clusters into PbI 2 nanowires to achieve controllable morphology of the PbI 2 film. The nanowires act as scaffolds for the subsequent perovskite formation. An in-plane low-angle diffraction detected in the in-situ grazing-incidence small-angle X-ray scattering (GISAXS) for the PbI 2 film indicates the formation of a periodically arranged ordered structure. The PbI 2 nanowires facilitate the ion-exchange process, markedly improving the homogeneity and orientation of the perovskite films, which is confirmed by the in-situ grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS). As a result, a champion power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 26.94% (certified as 26.66%, a very high certification efficiency of n-i-p structured perovskite devices) is achieved for the laboratory area (aperture area of the mask is 0.0618 cm 2 ). Moreover, a micro module device with an aperture area of 21.54 cm 2 was successfully manufactured and achieved a PCE of 24.60% (certified as 24.02%).

item.title: IDPForge: deep learning of proteins with global and local regions of disorder
item.dc:creator: Stefano De Castro
Oufan Zhang
Zi Hao Liu
Julie D. Forman-Kay
Teresa Head-Gordon
item.description:
Authors: Stefano De Castro, Oufan Zhang, Zi Hao Liu, Julie D. Forman-Kay, Teresa Head-Gordon
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Although machine learning has transformed protein structure prediction of folded protein ground states with remarkable accuracy, intrinsically disordered proteins and regions (IDPs/IDRs) are defined by diverse and dynamical structural ensembles that are predicted with low confidence by algorithms such as AlphaFold and RoseTTAFold. We present a machine learning method, IDPForge ( I ntrinsically D isordered P rotein, FO lded and disordered R egion GE nerator), that exploits a transformer protein language diffusion model to create all-atom IDP ensembles and IDR ensembles that maintains the folded domains. IDPForge does not require sequence-specific training, back transformations from coarse-grained representations, nor ensemble reweighting. The created IDP/IDR conformational ensembles show good agreement with both NMR and SAXS solution experimental data, and options for biasing with experimental restraints are available if desired. IDPForge with these diverse capabilities facilitates integrative and structural studies for proteins that contain intrinsic disorder, and is available as an open source resource for general use.

item.title: Synthetic tools to redirect the ubiquitin E3 ligase activity of a plant-specific N-recognin
item.dc:creator: Keely E. A. Oldham
Suyan Yee
Kai Xun Chan
Peter D. Mabbitt
item.description:
Authors: Keely E. A. Oldham, Suyan Yee, Kai Xun Chan, Peter D. Mabbitt
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The Arg/N-degron pathway regulates important agronomic traits. In plants, the PROTEOLYSIS 1 (PRT1) protein binds to aromatic amino-terminal residues and recruits ubiquitin (Ub) conjugating enzymes to ubiquitinate substrate proteins. Here, we demonstrate that PRT1 recruits the UBC35-UEV1A complex via RING1 of PRT1. This stimulates UBC35 to produce K63-linked Ub chains. To afford chemical control over Ub signalling, we construct a synthetic substrate of PRT1 with an N-terminal calmodulin-binding peptide (CBP). The addition of the CBP sequence to the substrate creates an off switch for PRT1-dependent ubiquitination that is regulated by calcium and calmodulin. Finally, we produce a set of nanobodies that are recognised by PRT1 and induce the ubiquitination of a reporter protein. Altogether, we introduce and biochemically validate several tools to both redirect and chemically control the Arg/N-degron pathway.

item.title: Sequential protonation and deprotonation reactions govern alternating access in a Major Facilitator Superfamily proton/multidrug antiporter
item.dc:creator: Sana Khalid
Himansha Singh
Keiko Shinoda
Xiaofen Lin
Hendrik W. van Veen
item.description:
Authors: Sana Khalid, Himansha Singh, Keiko Shinoda, Xiaofen Lin, Hendrik W. van Veen
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Drug/proton antiporters of the Major Facilitator Superfamily are key drivers of antimicrobial resistance. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying proton-coupled drug efflux are inherently complex and remain unresolved. Here, we dissect the timing and mechanism of proton coupling in the multidrug transporter LmrP, a prototypical exporter of clinically relevant antibiotics and toxins. By directly tracking chamber opening in the native plasma membrane, we capture functionally relevant conformational transitions within a lipid environment and map them onto the catalytic carboxylates that govern transport. Our results suggest that earlier DEER distance measurements in detergent solution captured a restricted subset of conformational states, which our pH 8.0 data extend and place into a broader framework. Complementary pH 5.0 measurements reveal additional mechanistic features and, together, these datasets define the transport cycle in a membrane-embedded context. Supported by molecular dynamics simulations, the results reveal a coordinated, transport cycle-dependent mechanism in which paired catalytic carboxylates act sequentially in substrate binding, proton relay, gate control, and transporter resetting.

item.dc:creator: Paul M. Leidinger

item.description:
Authors: Paul M. Leidinger, Silvia Mauri, Piero Torelli, Benedikt Buhk, Vitaly L. Sushkevich, Jeppe V. Lauritsen, Jeroen A. van Bokhoven, Luca Artiglia
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The hydrogenation of carbon dioxide to value-added chemicals is a major challenge. Metal-oxide interfaces and surface structures play fundamental roles and govern the selectivity of this reaction; thus, catalysts must be investigated under relevant reaction conditions to identify structure-activity relationships and engineer more efficient materials. This work aims to elucidate mechanisms of carbon dioxide hydrogenation to methanol and side products by using operando characterization techniques within a pressure range of 1 mbar up to 15 bar. Bifunctional Ag/ZnO and Ag/ZnO:Al 2 O 3 catalysts are studied using multiple spectroscopic techniques combined with online product analysis. During catalyst activation in hydrogen, several restructuring processes of the catalyst occur at different pressures. Under carbon dioxide hydrogenation reaction conditions carbonate, formate and CH x surface intermediates show strong pressure-dependent abundances. Combining thermodynamics with in situ and operando investigations of pressure-dependent structures and intermediates allows assessing carbon dioxide hydrogenation through the pressure gap.

item.title: Process-dependent shifts in conspecific negative density dependence during boreal forest succession
item.dc:creator: Yingying Zhu
Chen Chen
Han Y. H. Chen
item.description:
Authors: Yingying Zhu, Chen Chen, Han Y. H. Chen
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Conspecific negative density dependence (CNDD)—the stronger negative effects of conspecific than heterospecific neighbours on plant demographic performance—is a key process proposed to stabilize forest diversity, yet how it changes during succession remains poorly understood. Using a 25-year spatially explicit dataset from 148 post-fire plots in boreal forests, we show that species richness increases with stand age and that CNDD varies in process- and abundance-dependent ways across recruitment, survival, and growth. Plot-level CNDD shows no significant change with stand age in recruitment or survival, but mean relative effects are generally stronger for recruitment, and CNDD shifts from destabilizing to stabilizing for growth as stands mature. Species-level CNDD is strongly associated with species abundance, with rare species consistently experiencing stronger CNDD in recruitment and growth, whereas common species tend toward neutral or destabilizing effects. For survival, by contrast, CNDD is stronger in common than in rare species. These abundance-related differences remain broadly consistent across stand development, except in recruitment, where CNDD intensifies in rare species but remains consistently weak or near-neutral in common species. This shifting balance of density-dependent pressures highlights succession-driven trade-offs as central to species coexistence and increases in diversity in disturbance-driven forests.

item.title: Video-rate volumetric chemical imaging via mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography
item.dc:creator: Masato Fukushima
Keiichiro Toda
Yusei Sugawara
Shotaro Kawano
Takuro Ideguchi
item.description:
Authors: Masato Fukushima, Keiichiro Toda, Yusei Sugawara, Shotaro Kawano, Takuro Ideguchi
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11075
Abstract: Abstract Label-free vibrational microscopy provides chemically specific access to cellular structures, yet quantitative volumetric imaging of intracellular dynamics remains challenging on subsecond timescales. Here, we demonstrate video-rate mid-infrared photothermal optical diffraction tomography (MIP-ODT) by combining high photothermal sensitivity with rapid angular scanning. The system achieves 19.2 volumes per second, nearly 400 times faster than previous MIP tomography implementations, with a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 70 and no temporal averaging. We track lipid droplets in living cells and quantify anomalous diffusion from three-dimensional trajectories, revealing heterogeneous intracellular transport behaviors obscured in two-dimensional measurements. Rapid mid-infrared wavenumber sweeping further enables broadband multi-wavenumber volumetric chemical imaging across a 300 cm⁻¹ spectral window within 1 s. These results establish MIP-ODT as a platform for high-speed, label-free volumetric chemical imaging of single cells and quantitative investigation of dynamic intracellular organization.

item.title: Genomic heterogeneity inflates the performance of variant pathogenicity predictions
item.dc:creator: Baiyu Lu
Xueshen Liu
Po-Yu Lin
Nadav Brandes
item.description:
Authors: Baiyu Lu, Xueshen Liu, Po-Yu Lin, Nadav Brandes
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Recent studies have reported unprecedented accuracy predicting pathogenic variants across the genome, including in noncoding regions, using large deep-learning models trained on vast genomic data. To verify and understand the basis of these reports, we systematically evaluated the prediction accuracy of frontier models over single-nucleotide variants, focusing on general models capable of scoring multiple variant types across coding or noncoding regions. Our evaluations reveal that the performance of genome-wide predictions is severely inflated by mixing variant categories with different baseline prevalences of pathogenic variants. We constructed a benchmark stratified by variant type to identify the best-performing models for each genomic context, determine where reliable predictions remain out of reach, and establish rigorous standards to guide future evaluations.

item.title: Ligand hardness as a key feature differentiating base- versus noble-metal mechanisms of nickel-catalyzed Suzuki-Miyaura cross-couplings

Erin M. Eason

Tamal Das

item.description:
Authors: Anjali S. Bardhan, Erin M. Eason, Claire A. Herbert, Tamal Das, Andrew D. Cypcar, Jenny Y. Yang, Jennifer S. Hirschi, Elizabeth R. Jarvo
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Nickel-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions that engage alkyl electrophiles provide potential routes for synthesis of molecules with high F sp3 . However, development of these reactions remains a challenge since the impact of ligand identity on competing mechanistic pathways is not yet well understood. To address this knowledge gap, we establish structure-reactivity trends across >550 Suzuki-Miyaura cross-coupling reactions with known mechanistic pathways. We evaluate reaction outcome by ligand features including heteroatom identity, hybridization, bite angle, geometry, and buried volume. The most important determinant of reactivity is heteroatom identity: nitrogen-based ligands support open-shell reactions while phosphorus-based ligands support closed-shell reactions. Here we report that experimental and calculated reduction potentials and charge density analysis correlate with catalytic activity and propose a rationale for these observations based on hard-soft acid-base theory.

item.title: A combinatorial genetics approach reveals limits to redundancy within Plasmodium falciparum invasion ligand families
item.dc:creator: Eleanor Silvester
Anna Kuroshchenkova
Carla Briggs
Alazhar Colombowala
Victor Flores
Emma Kals
Julian C. Rayner
item.description:
Authors: Eleanor Silvester, Anna Kuroshchenkova, Carla Briggs, Alazhar Colombowala, Victor Flores, Emma Kals, Julian C. Rayner
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract To maintain infection in the human bloodstream, Plasmodium falciparum parasites undergo repeated cycles of invasion of and multiplication inside red blood cells (RBCs). Two protein families, the Erythrocyte binding-like (EBA) and Reticulocyte binding-like (Rh) proteins, are known to play a key role in invasion, mediating early stages of attachment of the P. falciparum merozoite to the host RBC. There is a degree of redundancy within these families, such that disrupting the function of individual EBA/Rh proteins in vitro is not sufficient to prevent invasion. By employing a novel approach to disrupt multiple EBA and Rh genes in combination, we systematically assess functional interdependency across these families for the first time. This analysis, and further characterisation of mutant parasites, reveals that disruption of some pairs of EBA/Rh ligands significantly impacts P. falciparum invasion, whereas others do not. Disruption of PfEBA175 in combination with either PfRh2b or PfRh4 significantly reduces parasite multiplication in vitro, indicating that the remaining EBA/Rh proteins cannot fully compensate for the absence of these three key invasion ligands. PfEBA175, PfRh2b and PfRh4 may therefore represent a critical nexus of the parasite invasion machinery, and combinatorial approaches that target these specific ligands could be a beneficial therapeutic approach.

item.title: Precise modular engineering of neutral organometallic rectangles from binuclear palladacycles via hierarchical assembly strategy
item.dc:creator: Yanzhe Ma
Lixin Duan
Tianheng Hou
Jiaxin Zhang
Haonan Sun
Ran Ma
Tao Tu
item.description:
Authors: Yanzhe Ma, Lixin Duan, Tianheng Hou, Jiaxin Zhang, Haonan Sun, Ran Ma, Tao Tu
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Metallosupramolecular assembly provides a powerful strategy for the precise construction of well-defined architectures with diverse topologies and functionalities. However, the construction of neutral organometallic architectures supported by robust metal-carbon bonds remains underdeveloped, largely because kinetic persistence limits the reversible structural correction required for conventional self-assembly. Herein, we employ binuclear palladacycles as intrinsically neutral and geometrically preorganized building blocks and develop a hierarchical assembly strategy that temporally separates geometric programming, scaffold editing, and topology locking. Through a polymerization-cleavage-assembly process, cyclopalladated polymers are converted into discrete binuclear precursors while retaining their programmed geometrical information. Subsequent trans-effect-directed N -heterocyclic carbene ligation affords a series of size-tunable, kinetically robust, and neutral organometallic rectangles. The resulting architectures are fully characterized by spectroscopic methods and single crystal X-ray diffraction analyses. Moreover, single crystal X-ray diffraction identifies guest-mediated breathing-like geometric deformations in the solid state, driven by exo-wall π-π stacking and charge-transfer interactions with both electron-rich and electron-deficient planar guests. This work establishes a hierarchical construction principle for accessing discrete neutral organometallic architectures by separating geometric programming from the final locking of the topology through strong bond formation, while demonstrating that local geometric adaptation can occur without disrupting the framework connectivity established by Pd-C bonds.

item.title: Genomic surveillance meets clinical practice: rule-based individualized treatment prediction for gonorrhoea using SensiTyper
item.dc:creator: Daniel Golparian
Leonor Sánchez-Busó
Magnus Unemo
item.description:
Authors: Daniel Golparian, Leonor Sánchez-Busó, Magnus Unemo
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11293
Abstract: Abstract Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

item.description:
Authors: Andrea Torchi, Joanne E. Mallinson, Stephen Bawden, Jordan J. McGing, Dileep N. Lobo, Andrew Cooper, Matthias Glaser, Frazer Twyman, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Skeletal muscle undergoes rapid and dynamic changes in energy demand during exercise, limiting the physiological relevance of resting-state measurements. Here, we demonstrate the feasibility of combining hyperpolarised ¹³C magnetic resonance spectroscopy (¹³C-MRS) with ³¹P-MRS to non-invasively measure real-time metabolic responses in exercising human skeletal muscle. Sedentary and endurance-trained men perform plantar-flexion exercise inside a magnetic resonance scanner. Dynamic hyperpolarised [1-¹³C]pyruvate spectra from the medial gastrocnemius show that increasing exercise intensity escalates pyruvate-to-lactate conversion relative to mitochondrial pyruvate utilisation. Endurance training is associated with greater bicarbonate labelling, consistent with increased mitochondrial pyruvate utilisation, and reduced lactate production. These metabolic signatures are accompanied by intensity- and training-dependent differences in phosphocreatine degradation and intracellular pH decline measured by ³¹P-MRS. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of combining hyperpolarised ¹³C- and ³¹P-MRS to phenotype skeletal muscle metabolism during exercise, providing a platform for investigating metabolic adaptations in ageing, disease and therapeutic intervention.

item.description:
Authors: Joy S. Xiang, Karen X. Zhao, Laliv Tadri, Kurt Tamaru, Brian A. Yee, Katherine Rothamel, Jonathan C. Schmok, Jasmine R. Mueller, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The global impact of the COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need for a deeper understanding of SARS-CoV-2 replication. Although the essential roles of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (NSP12), primase (NSP8), and nucleocapsid (N) proteins are established, their contact points with the full-length viral RNA genome during active infection require further characterization. We mapped NSP8 and NSP12 binding to the 5′ and 3′ ends of positive- and negative-sense RNA, consistent with their roles in viral replication, transcription, and translation. We also observed an NSP12 binding site within the conserved Y1 domain of NSP3 that modulates RNA and protein abundance. In addition, N binds the 5′ untranslated region (UTR), supporting a role in translational regulation early in infection, and associates with the frameshift element, where it modulates ribosomal frameshifting. Together, these findings map SARS-CoV-2 RNA–protein interactions across the viral genome and delineate specific regulatory regions for potential antiviral intervention.

Abstract: Abstract Programmable terahertz (THz) metasurfaces have emerged as a versatile platform for dynamic wavefront control, offering possibilities for high-capacity wireless communication and advanced sensing. Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Spirochetes are spiral-shaped bacteria whose curved periplasmic flagella drive corkscrew-like motility through viscous environments. Abstract: Abstract Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep degrades with age, and more severely in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). REM sleep comprises about twenty percent of adult sleep, alternates between phasic and tonic periods, and includes delta waves (1-4 Hz) in two forms: fast sawtooth waves and slower, NREM-like waves, whose expression dynamically varies across REM periods. Moreover, variation in APOE alleles, a major genetic risk factor for AD, was independently associated with a reduction in fast sawtooth wave density, thereby linking a genetic predisposition for AD to these specific REM microstructural changes. These findings identify a signature of memory decline in aging and implicate REM sleep as a distinct vulnerable substrate through which AD pathology may impair brain function.

item.title: CryoET imaging reveals that mitotic spindles are locally organized by microtubule density and Eg5 activity
item.dc:creator: William Conway
Daija Bobe
Vitaly Zimyanin
Gunar Fabig
Alex de Marco
Stefanie Redemann
item.description:
Authors: William Conway, Daija Bobe, Vitaly Zimyanin, Gunar Fabig, Alex de Marco, Stefanie Redemann
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract When eukaryotic cells divide, a mitotic spindle, composed of microtubule filaments interacting with molecular motors, self-assembles and is responsible for aligning and segregating chromosomes to the opposite daughter cells. Recent structural studies revealed that spindles are composed of short microtubules that do not span the full pole-to-chromosome distance. It remains unclear how these short, disconnected microtubules collectively assemble a bipolar spindle. Using cryo-electron tomography to map microtubule polarity in human spindles, we find that microtubules organize with consistent 8 nm wall-to-wall spacing. Spacing scales inversely with local microtubule density, consistent with organization by density-driven steric interactions, analogous to liquid crystal ordering. We find that the Eg5 motor establishes local antiparallel overlap independently of spindle bipolarity, while a balance of Eg5 and dynein regulates microtubule density to maintain spindle architecture. Together, these findings reveal the mesoscale principles by which cells build complex, self-healing cellular architectures from nanoscale building blocks.

item.dc:creator: Xingxing Zhong
Mian Wei

item.description:
Authors: Xingxing Zhong, Mian Wei, Jing-Kai Wang, Yuqing Zhang, Xiaoyan Jiang, Jianhua Yu, Xiang Zhao
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The pore-space-partition (PSP) has been recognized as a powerful strategy for boosting the uptake capacity of small gas molecules and has seen wide application in reticular chemistry. However, the most successful PSP platform—the partitioned- acs (pacs) net—has followed only one pattern since its inception over a decade ago: one partition agent per partition site, with a general formula of [M 3 O( L1 ) 3 ]( L2 ). This fully partitioned architecture occupies all metal sites, eliminating open metal sites (OMSs) and compromising selectivity. Herein, we introduce a partial PSP concept accessed through a framework desymmetrization strategy. By replacing traditional high-symmetry D 2h ligands with lower-symmetry C 2h ligands (e.g., fumaric acid), we introduce structural distortions into the acs network, breaking the uniformity of partition sites and allowing partition agents to occupy only a fraction of available positions. This provides access to a PSP mechanism, namely part-pacs (partially partitioned- acs ), with a general formula of [M 3 O( L1 ) 3 ]( L2 ) 1/3 . The part-pacs structures retain high acetylene capacity while exhibiting significantly enhanced selectivity compared to their fully partitioned analogues. Specifically, part-pacs-fum-tpa achieves C 2 H 2 /CO 2 separation productivity nearly twice that of its full-pacs counterpart (1.92 mol kg −1 vs 0.98 mol kg −1 ).

item.title: Retarding efficiency loss upon scaling in perovskite photovoltaics as fill factor becomes the bottleneck
item.dc:creator: Buyi Yan
Ruihao Gong

item.description:
Authors: Buyi Yan, Ruihao Gong, Yanchun Huang, Nannan Gu, Runfeng Li, Dongxue Liu, Kangrong Yan, Xuehui Xu, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Perovskite solar cells approach crystalline-silicon efficiencies at small areas, yet substantial performance losses during scale-up hinder their translation into practical modules. Here we quantify the contributions of device-performance parameters to efficiency loss during scale-up across diverse perovskite technologies, identifying fill factor ( $${FF}$$ F F ) as a major contributor and target for mitigating this loss. Further analysis resolves the FF deficit into voltage-, diode-non-ideality- and transport-associated contributions. Cryo-controlled processing provides an experimental route to preserve $${FF}$$ F F by regulating intermediate-phase evolution during crystallization. The resulting $${FF}$$ F F -preservation advantage arises predominantly from reduced diode non-ideality, with the other contributions being smaller. This advantage increases across device scales. A mini-module (19.48 cm 2 aperture) achieves a record certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% with an $${FF}$$ F F of 83.3%, the highest reported for perovskite modules. The same $${FF}$$ F F limitation governs operational performance decay, linking efficiency retention during scale-up with long-term stability. Together, these results establish $${FF}$$ F F preservation and the factors governing it as central to mitigating performance loss during scale-up and operation.

item.title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
item.dc:creator: Declan A. Gray

item.description:
Authors: Declan A. Gray, Nguyen Thi Nhung, Roelof Dirk Coertze, Mutshiene Deogratias Ekwanzala, Noel Waters, Josef D. Järhult, Michaela Wenzel, Christina Åhrén, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 11162
Abstract: Abstract Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

Authors: Philipp Trolese, Benedetta Fongaro, Alberto Benetollo, Vittoria Scapin, Martina Scano, Elena Rampazzo, Alice Sosic, Dorianna Sandonà, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Proteolytic processing of α-Synuclein (Syn) contributes to the molecular diversity and toxicity of its aggregates in Parkinson’s disease, yet the proteases responsible for disease-relevant truncations remain incompletely defined. Here, we show that thrombin, a serine protease associated with inflammatory conditions, selectively cleaves Syn at Lys6–Gly7, generating a 7–140 fragment despite the presence of multiple potential cleavage sites. Cleavage is modulated by ionic strength and the conformational ensemble of Syn, with more extended states being preferentially cleaved. The resulting 7–140 fragment adopts a more compact conformational ensemble, delays the formation of aggregation-prone species, produces fibrils with altered morphology and shows reduced membrane-induced α-helix formation. Although 7–140 aggregates are modestly less toxic, the truncation also impairs physiological functions of the protein. These findings describe a mechanism by which an inflammation-associated protease, thrombin, may contribute to Parkinson’s disease by selectively modifying Syn structure, aggregation and function.

item.dc:creator: R. Blake Richardson

item.description:
Authors: R. Blake Richardson, Caroline Kikawa, Amit Garg, Eva Bednarski, Madihah Salim, David J. Bacsik, Ethan C. Veit, Anna Hermacinski, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract The flavivirus nonstructural protein 5 performs multiple functions during infection, including RNA replication and type I interferon signaling antagonism. Although flavivirus NS5 proteins inhibit IFN signaling through distinct mechanisms, which suggests evolutionary flexibility, the evolutionary constraints for these activities to coexist within a single protein remain to be determined. Here, we map the Zika virus NS5 STAT2 antagonism determinants and compare them with replication constraints defined by deep mutational scanning. Antagonism and replication determinants extensively overlap, and no single amino acid substitution eliminates antagonism without impairing replication. Resolving these fitness landscapes in parallel identifies specific combinations of partially functional substitutions that retain replication capacity while markedly reducing antagonism. These viruses are profoundly attenuated in human STAT2 knock-in mice. Our results uncover a fundamental evolutionary constraint linking replication and immune evasion activities in NS5, highlight that STAT2 antagonism is essential for ZIKV pathogenesis and provide new avenues for attenuated ZIKV vaccines.

item.title: Evolutionary oxidation of proteins in Earth’s history
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey M. Dick
Jingqiang Tan
Hongchen Jiang
Douglas E. LaRowe
item.description:
Authors: Jeffrey M. Dick, Jingqiang Tan, Hongchen Jiang, Douglas E. LaRowe
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Evidence for Earth’s oxygenation during the Great Oxidation Event (GOE) and Neoproterozoic Oxidation Event (NOE) comes primarily from the geological record. We report rising oxidation state of carbon (Zc) in proteins over billion-year timescales, a consistent trend recovered from diverse genomic datasets. Combining statistical and thermodynamic modeling, we link this trend to environmental drivers including Earth’s progressive oxygenation and secular cooling. The oxidation trend appears in the amino acid composition of modern genomes from methanogens and sulfur-cycling organisms, phylostratigraphic gene age groups in eukaryotes, and reconstructed ancestral sequences for Rubisco, nitrogenase, thioredoxin, and 3-isopropylmalate dehydrogenase (IPMDH). Major Zc steps broadly overlap the GOE but do not exactly coincide with it; uncertainties in phylogenetic age and limited spatial associations complicate direct comparison with geochemical proxies. Gene age groups in unicellular, but not multicellular, eukaryotes show a second rise of protein Zc around the NOE. These widespread genomic signatures of protein oxidation are consistent with a thermodynamic hypothesis in which energy minimization directs protein sequence evolution across metabolic functions.

Authors: Aina Karen Anthi, Daniela Bejan, Simone Mester, Nijaguna Bethur, Elena Gonzalo-Gil, Sopisa Benjakul, Kristin Hovden Aaen, Tilman Schlothauer, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10780
Abstract: Abstract Erythropoietin (EPO) products stimulate production of erythrocytes in patients with anemia. The drugs are delivered intravenously or subcutaneously up to several times per week due to short plasma half-life. Improving the pharmacokinetic properties of EPO will allow less frequent administration, and thus impact therapeutic utility and patient compliance. In this study, we took advantage of an albumin variant (QMP) engineered for improved engagement of FcRn, a key regulator of the plasma half-life of albumin. After genetic coupling of EPO to QMP, the fusion protein shows favorable neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) binding, and 5.2-fold prolonged plasma half-life in human FcRn expressing mice upon intravenous administration, when comparing with EPO fused to WT albumin, with a similar half-life obtained following subcutaneous administration. Importantly, both fusions bind the EPO receptor with binding kinetics equal to that of the product darbepoetin alfa. After intravenous administration, mice receiving darbepoetin alfa experiences a faster drop in EPO levels compared to those given EPO-QMP, and moreover, we measure a prolonged increase in erythrocytes with EPO-QMP. Furthermore, intranasal administration results in 5-fold higher circulating amounts of EPO-QMP and a prolonged increase in erythrocytes compared to darbepoetin alfa. Thus, long-acting EPO-QMP could be an attractive design to explore for both invasive and non-invasive delivery to patients with anemia.

item.title: Detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction with a gate-tunable van der Waals tunneling photodetector

item.description:
Authors: Kening Xiao, Xingsi Liu, Libo Zhang, Jintao Fu, Yiran Tan, Xin Li, Wenqi Mo, Bolang Peng, et al.
Journal: Nature Communications
Abstract: Abstract Cross-spectral prediction infers information in one spectral band from observations acquired in another. This task is ill-posed because multiple target-band signals can be compatible with a single source observation. Image-space supervision alone does not test consistency with a measured detector response. Here, we incorporate the calibrated response manifold of a gate-tunable PdSe 2 /h-BN/WSe 2 photodetector as a differentiable detector-response layer. Parameterized by wavelength, optical power, source-drain bias and gate voltage, this layer constrains the magnitude and polarity of the predicted detector response while preserving image fidelity. In visible-to-infrared cross-spectral prediction, the framework achieves a peak signal-to-noise ratio of 26.58 dB and a structural similarity index of 0.89. It also reduces detector-space error relative to architecture-only and response-corrupted controls. Post-inference measurements further evaluate 64-mask response consistency after 1310 nm optical re-encoding. These results establish detector-mediated cross-spectral prediction as a framework that combines image reconstruction with measured response-space consistency under the tested conditions.

Authors: Mikihito Noguchi, Kenta Suzuki, Hiroaki Fujita, Hirokazu Toju
Journal: Nature Communications; Volume: 17; Issue: 1; Article number: 10997
Abstract: Abstract Root-associated fungi and bacteria play pivotal roles in terrestrial ecosystem processes. However, identifying keystone taxa driving below-ground microbial assembly remains a major challenge. Here, we present a statistical framework for identifying microbes that reorganize microbiome assembly. Using 1,270 root samples collected from a cool-temperate forest in Japan, we reconstruct assembly landscapes describing the probabilistic structure of community states. We then find that several endophytic fungi (e.g., Phialocephala and Oidiodendron ) are strongly associated with the reorganization of assembly landscape topography along abundance gradients, coinciding with shifts in mycorrhizal symbiosis. Independent datasets from Europe confirm that the highlighted genera are significantly associated with changes in mycorrhizal colonization patterns. Prokaryotic communities exhibit transitions among states characterized by core taxa, Pseudomonadota, or Actinomycetota, strongly associated with abundance gradients of Candidatus Udaeobacter and several endophytic fungi. These findings provide a scalable framework for prioritizing candidate keystone taxa and linking microbiome assembly to ecosystem-scale processes.
